text: A pull-based agent applies manifests from Git, but nothing stops a human from reaching around it and changing the cluster directly. That gap between what's live and what's declared in Git is called drift, and this lesson covers how GitOps catches it and what it does next.

Picture an on-call engineer mid-incident running kubectl scale deployment payments-api --replicas=10 to handle a traffic spike. It works immediately, but now the live cluster says replicas: 10 while Git still says replicas: 5. Nobody opened a pull request, nobody committed anything, and the two no longer agree — the same thing happens with a hand-edited ConfigMap or a secret rotated outside the pipeline.

A GitOps agent doesn't apply manifests once and walk away. It runs a continuous reconciliation loop: read desired state from Git, read live state from the cluster, and if they differ, mark it drifted. That loop runs whether or not anyone touched Git recently, which is exactly what catches a manual kubectl scale. Argo CD surfaces this as an OutOfSync status; Flux exposes equivalent conditions you can read with kubectl describe.

Once drift is detected, the agent can either alert and let a human choose to re-sync or update Git, or self-heal — automatically re-applying Git's declared state and reverting the manual change on the next pass, which is what Argo CD's selfHeal setting does. Self-healing can undo a well-intentioned fix mid-incident, which is exactly why the right move during an incident is to commit the real fix to Git immediately instead of fighting the reconciler.

This is OpenGitOps's fourth principle, Continuously Reconciled: agents continuously observe actual state and attempt to apply desired state, not just at deploy time. Put all four principles together — declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled — and that's the complete definition of GitOps. Next lesson lines that definition up against a plain CI/CD pipeline to see exactly what changes.
